s10.old: - The task's hypothesis was half wrong: it said `time.time()` is precise and file stamps are coarse. Under Python 3.12.10 (what `python`, the kernel and both Disabled scheduled tasks (`Python312\pythonw.exe`) run) `time.time()` is `GetSystemTimeAsFileTime`, the SAME coarse tick NTFS stamps with: the file's nanosecond stamp was never below the clock's in 3,000 writes. The inversion lives in floats: `time.time()` is `ns/1e9`, `st_mtime` is `sec + 1e-9*nsec`, and for one instant they differ by exactly one float step (2.384e-07 s) in 13.4% of instants each way. Under 3.14.5 (the `py` launcher default here) `time.time()` is `GetSystemTimePreciseAsFileTime` and the hypothesis holds: stamps up to 9.5 ms older, 4 of 1,500 replayed launches failed. Coarse-behind-precise lag: median 4.4 ms, p99 15.3 ms, max 19.33 ms.
s10.why: "never below the clock's" is a number comparison

s10.old: - A fourth comparison nobody listed: line 194. `started_at` comes from `datetime.now()`, floored to the microsecond, and reads 0.24 to 0.95 microseconds below `started_epoch` in the same tick. A three-clause fix (file times only) was green 30 of 30 with real fsync and is still WRONG; timing amplification exposed it (17 of 23 amplified failures were the line 194 message). Fix = one-second tolerance on all four completion checks.
s10.why: "0.24 to 0.95 microseconds below started_epoch" is a number comparison
